title: Three Roots with Product One
statement: Let $U$ be the set of the $151$ complex numbers $z$ with $z^{151} = 1$. How many $3$-element subsets $\{u, v, w\}$ of $U$ satisfy both $uvw = 1$ and $|u + v + w| < 1$?
hints: Draw $u$, $v$ and $w$ on the unit circle and look at the three arcs into which they cut it. Find how $|u + v + w|$ depends on these arcs, and leave the condition $uvw = 1$ until the end.

For numbers of modulus $1$, $uv + vw + wu = uvw \cdot \overline{u + v + w}$, which gives $(u + v)(v + w)(w + u) = uvw\left(|u + v + w|^2 - 1\right)$. Writing each factor such as $u + v$ through the half-angle of the arc between $u$ and $v$ shows that $|u + v + w| < 1$ exactly when every arc is shorter than a semicircle.

Rotating a subset, that is, multiplying all three elements by the same $\zeta \in U$, keeps its arcs and multiplies its product by $\zeta^3$. Since $3$ is invertible modulo $151$, each class of $151$ rotated copies contains exactly one subset with product $1$. So count all $3$-element subsets of $U$ with every arc shorter than a semicircle, and divide by $151$.
solution:
Write $u = e^{i\alpha}$, $v = e^{i\beta}$ and $w = e^{i\gamma}$ with $\alpha < \beta < \gamma < \alpha + 2\pi$, and let $p = \beta - \alpha$, $q = \gamma - \beta$ and $r = 2\pi - (\gamma - \alpha)$ be the three arcs, so that $p, q, r > 0$ and $p + q + r = 2\pi$.

Since $|u| = |v| = |w| = 1$, we have $uv + vw + wu = uvw\,(\bar w + \bar u + \bar v) = uvw \cdot \overline{u + v + w}$, and therefore $$(u + v)(v + w)(w + u) = (u + v + w)(uv + vw + wu) - uvw = uvw\left(|u + v + w|^2 - 1\right).$$ On the other hand $u + v = 2\cos\frac{p}{2}\, e^{i(\alpha + \beta)/2}$, $v + w = 2\cos\frac{q}{2}\, e^{i(\beta + \gamma)/2}$ and $w + u = 2\cos\frac{p + q}{2}\, e^{i(\gamma + \alpha)/2}$, and the product of the three exponentials is $e^{i(\alpha + \beta + \gamma)} = uvw$. As $\cos\frac{p + q}{2} = \cos\left(\pi - \frac{r}{2}\right) = -\cos\frac{r}{2}$, comparing the two expressions gives $$|u + v + w|^2 - 1 = -8\cos\dfrac{p}{2}\cos\dfrac{q}{2}\cos\dfrac{r}{2}.$$

Each arc is a multiple of $\frac{2\pi}{151}$, so no arc equals $\pi$, and at most one arc exceeds $\pi$. If all three arcs are less than $\pi$, the product of the cosines is positive and $|u + v + w| < 1$. If one arc exceeds $\pi$, exactly one cosine is negative and $|u + v + w| > 1$. So the condition $|u + v + w| < 1$ says that every arc is shorter than a semicircle, that is, at most $75$ steps of $\frac{2\pi}{151}$.

First count the $3$-element subsets of $U$ with this property, ignoring the product. A subset fails exactly when it has an arc of at least $76$ steps. Such an arc is unique; let $u$ be the element at its anticlockwise end. Then the other two elements lie among the $75$ elements that follow $u$ anticlockwise, and conversely any such choice gives a failing subset. So $151\binom{75}{2}$ subsets fail, and the number with every arc shorter than a semicircle is $$\binom{151}{3} - 151\binom{75}{2} = 562475 - 151 \cdot 2775 = 562475 - 419025 = 143450.$$

Now bring in the product. Let $\zeta = e^{2\pi i/151}$. Multiplying all elements of a subset by $\zeta^t$ keeps its arcs and multiplies its product by $\zeta^{3t}$. For $t = 1, \dots, 150$ this rotation moves the elements of $U$ in a single cycle of length $151$, because $151$ is prime, so it fixes no $3$-element subset. Hence the subsets fall into classes of $151$ rotated copies with the same arcs, and in a class whose first member has product $\zeta^s$ the products are $\zeta^{s + 3t}$ for $t = 0, 1, \dots, 150$. As $\gcd(3, 151) = 1$, these are all $151$ elements of $U$, each once, so exactly one subset in each class has product $1$.

Therefore the number of subsets with $uvw = 1$ and $|u + v + w| < 1$ is $\frac{143450}{151} = 950$.
